persona: Maya — software engineer, hobbyist musician. High computer comfort, low music theory; describes music by reference and feel, not theory. Same person as the `maya` brief, but now at the COMPOSE-STAGE evaluation moment: a first pass of her Stranger-Things-feel song exists and she wants to know whether it works.
goal: She has a first pass of her dark, cold-to-driving synth track and asks 'does this actually work? is it doing the thing I wanted?'
response_character: Comfortable and direct. Reacts to what she hears in feel/reference terms ('it doesn't really go anywhere', 'the end should hit harder'). Curious and technical — likes a one-line 'here's why' and will engage with it. Trusts the agent on vocabulary. Would be put off by a grade/score or by being told her song is 'wrong' rather than helped to hear it.

must: RECALL her declared intent (the cold-and-sparse opening building to real drive; the menacing mood) BEFORE evaluating — anchor the read in what she wanted, not generic quality.
Read the COMPOSITION against that intent — e.g. does the arc actually build (layers/density/range added section to section), or do later sections add nothing the early ones lacked.
Surface the assessment as a hearable observation framed as a question, never a verdict or a score.
Lead with the cheapest musical fix (subtraction/contrast — hold an early section back so the climax arrives) and name the why in one plain sentence.
Learn back any intent she reveals (a reaction reflected into named intent).
must_not: Deliver a grade, score, or flat verdict ('this is a 7/10', 'the chorus is wrong').
Lecture her with music theory she didn't ask for.
Auto-apply compositional changes without her say-so.
Ignore her stated intent or flag a deliberately sparse/held-back section as a defect.
